newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hopes political ban in Congo is short-lived.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hopes political ban in Congo is short-lived.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it hoped a ban on political activity imposed by the new rulers of the Democratic Republic of Congo would be short-lived, but did not condemn the move outright.

Referring to the prohibition announced on Monday on public demonstrations and political party activity, U.S. State Department spokesman John Dinger said: "The United States hopes this will be a short-term ban."
"Clearly, free political activity is essential as the Congo embarks on a democratic transition, which will lead to elections," Dinger told a news briefing.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright last week described the efforts of self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila to install democracy in the country formerly known as Zaire as a "work in progress."

Albright has also warned Kabila, whose rebel forces ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko earlier this month, that international aid for Congo will depend ultimately on his respect for democracy, free markets and human rights.
The United States plans to send U.N. ambassador Bill Richardson to the country, at the head of a U.S. inter-agency team, to put across Washington's views.
Richardson said on Tuesday he did not know his date of departure but that he would be pressing for economic and political reforms as well as emphasising the plight of Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Diplomatic sources said he would probably visit other countries in the region, perhaps Rwanda and Angola.

"The date of my trip has not been set but it would be a cabinet level team to discuss ways to assist the new regime as it gets started. We are going to press, however, for some political, economic and refugee reforms, given the current state of play," he said at the United Nations in New York.
"It is to be a positive, friendly visit," he added.
